articles.title: Breaking the silence: Pratishta’s journey from childhood abuse to advocacy
articles.author: Susmita Aryal
paras: In South Asia, survivors of sexual and physical abuse are often met with judgment and stigma
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.
Editorial note: This article contains mention of gender-based violence, sexual assault, violence against children, and child sexual abuse, which may be triggering for some readers.

November 25 to December 10, 2026, marks the UN’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. However, even as gender-based violence gets more recognition globally, survivors are still struggling to access social or legal justice. South Asia is no exception to this. Global Voices sat down with one survivor of childhood abuse who uses her experience to fuel her advocacy work today.

South Asia is home to nearly one quarter of the world’s population, woven with a diverse, culture-driven fabric where women are often celebrated as goddesses. However, this veneration doesn’t necessarily mean South Asian women are safe or free from abuse.

In Nepal, there are far too many examples of crimes against women and girls. For instance, Nirmala Panta, 13, was found dead in a sugarcane field — a case which has remained unsolved since 2018. Bhagirathi Bhatta, 17, was choked to death when returning home from school in 2021, and Inisha BK, 16, was found unconscious in the Janagaran Community Forest in Surkhet in early 2026. A similar yet shocking case is that of a 3-year-old Garima, who was found dead inside an abandoned house in Jeetpur in southern Nepal. While these tragic rape and murder cases leave deep scars in Nepal’s national psyche, even more cases go unheard and unreported.

Sparking a nationwide outrage, such cases force the country to confront a collective shame. They raise questions around human morality, diminishing trust and affection in society, and breakdowns in the legal justice system. In the face of these atrocities, women took to the streets, demanding justice and accountability. But their calls fell on deaf ears.

“I was 11 years old when I was sexually abused by my close maternal uncle for four days,” said Pratishtha Gautam in an online interview with Global Voices in November 2026. Opening up about this incident was a real challenge for her, yet she was committed to sharing her story.

Her childhood was by no means easy. She moved regularly as a child, and at six years old, she was sent to her grandparent’s house for a year because her parents had to move away to address their employment needs. This separation made her feel neglected and she felt that her parents loved her younger brother more. This contributed to a sense of emotional distance and detachment from her family.

Later, at the age of 11, she was left in the care of her mother’s cousin while her younger brother was hospitalized and receiving medical treatment. It was during this time that she experienced sexual abuse at the hands of someone she had known and trusted as a family member, who took away her innocence.

After four days of abuse, she escaped when the abuser fled after she began calling out for help. Finally getting a chance to flee from danger, she “rushed to my room, quickly happened to lock the door by chance, thankfully, and began to scream out to my neighbors.” She had witnessed men mistreating women growing up and feels lucky that her cries weren’t met with indifference.
The abuse only compounded her challenges. As she says, “It was not easy at all.”

The experience has left her with scars: “I have been awakened with nightmares since that incident, making my sleep extremely difficult.” She also suffers from panic attacks when she sees material about sexual abuse. She describes feeling like her heart is swollen and being torn apart. When triggered, she often freezes up and dissociates.

According to research from the American Academy of Pediatrics journal, child sexual abuse can be incredibly detrimental to a person’s long-term mental well-being. Child abuse survivors are more likely to suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, eating disorders and disturbances, sleep disruption and insomnia, and dissociation, as well as adverse physical health conditions and attachment issues, according to the Center of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse.

This highlights the immense scale of pain that many children experience when they are victims of sexual abuse. Not everyone is able to speak out about such abuses. This is particularly true in South Asia, where there is a social stigma around abuse, due to entrenched ideas around “purity.”

She resents suggestions that it is women’s responsibility to not “tempt” men or draw attention to themselves. “Why should we be the ones to cover ourselves up?” she asks. She refuses to hide and stay silent while her abuser “is living free somewhere.” She refuses to remain invisible.

Even as many countries make strides in gender equality, gender-based violence continues to be a major issue. In a 2023 report, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly one in three (31.6 percent) of women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime — roughly 840 million women and girls.

At the root of gender-based violence lies a belief in male superiority. Not all men would openly endorse this belief, yet many see themselves as protectors of the women in their lives: their sisters, mothers, girlfriends, and wives. But this notion of protection is deeply flawed, especially when it comes at the cost of women’s freedom, mobility, access to opportunities, dreams, and agency.

Gautam recognizes this notion in her own upbringing. She had dreams of her own and was ready to chase them, but the universe had a different plan for her. She kept her independence through consistent stubbornness and determination.

Today, Gautam lives in Adelaide in South Australia. She suffers from complex PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and works as a mental health clinician helping other survivors of abuse. She reflected, in a heavy tone, on being a thousand miles away from home but safe and independent.
Gautam feeding a child. Image via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.

PTSD and insomnia aren’t the only consequences of her abuse. While she was once married, she struggled to cope with her trauma, and it negatively impacted her relationship, eventually leading to divorce.

As part of her treatment, Gautam has met regularly with psychotherapists over the years. Eventually, even that wasn’t enough. She put everything on hold for a year and gave herself time and space to focus on her mental health. She believes she would have difficulty living a normal life and still struggles with relationships. “I hate men. I used to hate them and still have trust issues,” she said.

Even as she struggles to process her own trauma, she also works to help others recover from abuse and offers pro bono psychological counseling. Being part of the solution has in some ways helped her heal. Her passion as a mental health clinician goes beyond her own individual experiences to the collective — a reminder to be empathetic as humans first.

While she primarily works in Australia, she is also committed to helping women back in her home country of Nepal. She has collaborated with Rakshya Nepal, an organization in Nepal that protects women and girls from sexual exploitation and trafficking.
Reflecting back on the choices she made, she said, “I cannot imagine if I could afford this luxury of mental space if I were not in Australia.”

This is also a testament to how South Asia treats survivors of sexual and physical abuse — even if they gather the courage to speak the truth, too often they are met with judgment and scorn. Part of this is due to limited regard for mental health, but it’s also about entrenched gender roles and strong societal expectations. There is a popular saying in Nepal reflecting these persistent gender dynamics: “timi ta chori manche ho ni” and “chora manche ho ni,” which roughly translates to “you are a girl, and boys will be boys.”

articles.title: Growing up displaced in Cameroon after ten years of conflict
articles.author: Cynthia Ebot Takang
paras: Over 223,700 children have dropped out of school in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest regions, while 2,463 schools are non-operational
Originally published on Global Voices
A general view of Buea's OIC Market in the Southwest Region of Cameroon, where displaced families sell goods to support their livelihoods. Photo by Cynthia Ebot Takang. Used with permission.

For children displaced by Cameroon’s ongoing armed Anglophone conflict, reaching safety has not ended the struggle. In Buea, the capital of Cameroon’s Southwest region, some children are balancing school with market trading to help their families survive.

“At least here in Buea, there are no gunshots, and we do not have to hide in the bush,” says 11-year-old Lorane in an interview with Global Voices, describing the relative safety his family found after fleeing their home in Cameroon’s conflict-affected Southwest Region.

The move brought the children to a calmer environment where they could resume schooling and live with less fear of armed violence. But leaving their communities also meant losing homes, familiar surroundings, friendships and, for some, years of education. In Buea, the struggle to rebuild family livelihoods has introduced another responsibility to their lives: helping their parents earn a living.
A safer place, but a childhood reshaped by displacement

The Anglophone crisis in Cameroon began in 2016, when teachers and lawyers began protesting over the perceived marginalization of English-language education and common-law systems, which they say favored French. This escalated into wider demonstrations and a government crackdown. In 2017, the situation deteriorated into armed conflict between government forces and separatist groups seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions as a state commonly referred to as Ambazonia. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that between 2.1 and 2.2 million people have been displaced due to the violence and insecurity.

At Buea’s OIC Market, children from displaced families sell bleach, puff-puff, plantains, ginger, garlic, and oranges, particularly during weekends and before school. Some travel from neighboring communities to help their parents sell goods, while others work around family-owned stalls.

For 14-year-old Joy, this means traveling from Mutengene to Buea on weekends to sell sachets of bleach. Her mother buys the bleach in bulk and repackages it into smaller sachets, which Joy sells for CFA 100 (about USD 0.17) each. She says daily sales can reach CFA 10,000–15,000 (about USD 16.81–25.21), helping support the household and her siblings.

Joy has been working since her family fled their village when she was in Class Five. “They were shooting guns in my village, so my mum had to bring us here so we could continue school,” she says. She has since become used to the routine, which allows her to contribute to the family while continuing her education.

For 14-year-old Sidoine, displacement meant losing four years of schooling. Her family fled Ekona after their house was burned while they were away at the farm. She remembers hiding in the bushes when they heard attacks were coming, unsure what would happen next. Her family eventually left their hometown, Ekona, for Buea, joining thousands of others who have had to rebuild their lives away from their roots. A well-wisher eventually helped her enroll in school in Buea.
Although the family sometimes visits their farm to collect food, it has not been possible to return permanently. Sidoine misses her former home and friends.
Rebuilding a family livelihood

For younger children, displacement has also changed family routines. Twelve-year-old Michelle sells plantains while waiting for his mother to return from church. His 11-year-old cousin, Lorane, sometimes accompanies him. The two help their parents attract customers, particularly on weekends.
They also miss people they left behind in Ekona, including their grandmother, who died during a raid as a result of the crisis.

Susan Achuagoh, a mother of five whose house was burned during the conflict, has had to rebuild her livelihood as an orange seller in Buea. She gives her children small quantities of oranges to sell while she remains at her stall. This helps supplement their family income.
“I sell oranges; I give them small things to walk around with while I stay at the stall,” she shared in an interview with Global Voices. “If they do not help like that, it will not go at all.”

Her children’s education was interrupted for more than three years during the conflict. Another mother, Mami Blessing, says her children’s schooling was also disrupted and that they now help her at the market as the family struggles to make ends meet.

Godiva Ndang epse Limene, Education and Partnerships Officer at Street Child UK-Cameroon, says the prolonged crisis in the Northwest and Southwest has increasingly become a crisis of childhood, affecting education, protection, and development.

Children exposed to armed violence, displacement, and repeated insecurity may experience anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and social withdrawal. Taking on economic responsibilities can add to these pressures. Ndang says work that takes up time needed for learning, rest, and play can affect children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and physical development.

She stresses that helping in a family business is not automatically child labor. The distinction depends on the child’s age, the nature and duration of the activity, the risks involved, and whether it interferes with education, health, rest, or development.

The right to education is only one of the rights affected. Children also have a right to rest, leisure, and play, as well as protection from economic exploitation. For those uprooted from their communities, maintaining friendships, participating in cultural life, and developing a sense of belonging are also important parts of growing up.
Learning spaces offer a route back to education

The scale of the disruption remains significant. Figures from the Regional Delegations of Basic Education cited by UNICEF in September 2026 show that 223,749 children were completely out of school in the Northwest and Southwest, while 2,463 schools were non-operational. Of these, 2,005 were in the Northwest and 458 in the Southwest.

To educate children in conflict-affected communities, local partners including TeenAlive, the Foundation for Inclusive Education (FIED), Strategic Humanitarian Services (SHUMAS), and the Authentique Memorial Empowerment Foundation (AMEF) support Mobile Neighborhood Learning Corners and Satellite Learning Corners. These are established in accessible locations such as village chiefs’ homes, churches, schools, and community verandas.

The program has supported close to 100 learning corners across the two regions. Other education interventions include help with school enrollment, uniforms, and learning materials, as well as Teaching at the Right Level, a tutoring program.

Street Child also combines education with other forms of support. Its girls’ resilience and empowerment work provides displaced adolescent girls with life skills, literacy, and vocational training, alongside start-up kits and mental health assistance. Its Play for Peace initiative, supported by the FIFA Foundation, uses sports to promote peace, health, and education in conflict-affected communities.

Ndang says children also need psychosocial support, safe learning environments, and opportunities to play and interact with their peers. She adds that helping caregivers rebuild their livelihoods matters because reducing economic pressure on families can lessen the burden on children.
Ambition despite displacement
Despite interruptions to their education and the responsibilities they have taken on, the children interviewed for this story continue to speak about their goals and ambitions.

Eliot, 14, who helps his mother sell oranges on weekends, wants to become an engineer. Sidoine hopes to study law, although she worries about the years she lost in school. Vickians, 12, who fled Lebialem and now studies computer science, wants to become a computer engineer.
On weekends, Vickians sells miondo, a cassava-based delicacy, with her parents. Her family continues to make sacrifices to keep her in school, and she remains determined to pursue her education.

At the start of the 2026–2027 academic year, Southwest Governor Bernard Okalia Bilai said the authorities wanted children across the region to have equal access to education and learning facilities, despite differences in school attendance between urban and rural communities. His remarks, reported in this September 2026 interview on the reopening of schools, underline the challenge facing the region: ensuring that displacement and insecurity do not determine whether children can access education.

articles.title: Reclaiming Indigenous culinary histories in Nepal
articles.author: Sanjib Chaudhary
paras: The dominant Nepali food narrative overlooks the diverse regional histories and culinary traditions of Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Timu khole, wild mushroom soup. Photo by Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end. As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.
The author in conversation with women's group members. Photo via Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.
The cover of The Lekhali Cookbook. Photo by Sanjib Chaudhary. Used with permission.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.
SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.

articles.title: Why fossil fuel-producing countries are stalling this crucial climate report
articles.author: Kathryn Bowen, Director, Melbourne Climate Futures and Professor - Environment, Climate and Global Health at Melbourne Climate Futures and Melbourne School of Population and Global Health, University of Melbourne, The University of Melbourne
paras: After a year of record-breaking weather and a “super” El Niño underway, there’s no doubt climate extremes are wreaking havoc across the globe.

For decades, scientists have warned us this would happen. Their research made the case for reducing fossil fuel dependence. And we’ve relied on their expertise to assess the severity and extent of climate change.

But a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries is now obstructing the publication of a key scientific report from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This threatens global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. And it has created deep concern at the COP31 climate summit, currently in its final hours in Turkey, also known as Türkiye.

First, it helps to understand why this report is so significant. The IPCC is the UN body for assessing the science related to climate change. Established in 1988, it provides political leaders with independent scientific assessments on climate change and strategies for response.

This panel has produced six pivotal reports to date, which have collated and reviewed the latest knowledge on climate change science. And over the past two years, more than 640 experts from around the world have been meeting to write the seventh.

The authors are leading researchers who volunteer their time. More than half of the authors working on the current seventh report, called the Seventh Assessment Report, or AR7, are from developing countries. I am a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports in the working group that looks at impacts, vulnerability and adaptation.
Work on this seventh report kicked off in December 2024, and its timeline for completion was never officially finalised.
Originally, the plan was for the seventh report to be released in 2028. But five countries are objecting to this timeline and pushing for a later release in 2029.
India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya and China are ostensibly arguing that countries from the global south lack the resources and capacity to meet the current deadline.
However, these countries also happen to be among the world’s largest fossil fuel producers.

If recent reports are anything to go by, the evidence of global warming in this seventh report is likely to be alarming. It will highlight the evidence for much greater action, including deep and urgent reduction in fossil fuel production and use.

Extending the release date means IPCC contributors would have even more information they would have to assess. This delay would increase, not alleviate, the demands of authorship and reviewing for those contributors from developing nations.

The disagreement resulted in the suspension of the latest IPCC meeting in October in Ethiopia, with no confirmed timeline for the report release or budget for 2027. This threatens the very existence of the IPCC.

Nations seeking delay argue that tight timelines are unfair to developing countries. But the least developed countries (LDC), a group comprised of 44 nations, expressed “deep disappointment” when the meeting in Ethiopia was suspended.
Every five years, the UN’s climate body does a global stocktake of how effectively the world is responding to climate change.

Intended to ramp up climate action, these stocktakes take a long hard look at the state of the planet, identify the gaps in our approach and suggest a path forward. To be truly effective, these must be based on the latest science.

Delaying the seventh report would mean the most recent science is not fed into the 2028 global stocktake. This has grave implications for future climate action, and any delay in our response could have catastrophic effects on the wellbeing of planetary and human health.
While major fossil-fuel-emitting countries often attempt to impede phaseout efforts, undermining the IPCC follows a recent trend of discrediting science for political ends.

After a UN report in September found that limiting global warming to 1.5°C was no longer possible, Saudi Arabia jumped to question the credibility of the science, contending the research was not peer-reviewed. In fact, the report had been written over the course of a year by 44 experts, and reviewed by a further 44.

Despite opposition to delaying the IPCC report, those pushing for it have remained unmoved at COP31. Speaking to media at the summit, former US Vice President Al Gore accused Saudi Arabia of trying to sabotage the IPCC’s work.
“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” he said.

At climate negotiations where the phrase “fossil fuels” is routinely vetoed from the text, finding a resolution to the IPCC issue has even broader implications. If countries can’t agree on this, how will nearly 200 countries agree on a robust final COP31 outcome?

While the clock ticks down on the COP31 negotiations, a resolution to the IPCC issue is unlikely in Turkey. However, it is hoped a timeline and budget can be nailed down at meetings in early December.

As the world’s most authoritative global body on climate change, the role the IPCC plays in driving climate action is critical to our future wellbeing. And the science in this seventh report will be fundamental to a truly effective global stocktake.

In a time when the world often feels divided, settling this issue amicably and in good faith would offer countries a much-needed reminder that we are capable of cooperation in pursuit of a better future.

articles.title: The ongoing efforts to get ecocide recognized at the International Criminal Court
articles.author: Sydney Allen
paras: Activists want to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment and punish those responsible for defiling it
Originally published on Global Voices

An aerial view of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, the largest marine oil spill in history. Under the proposed ICC amendment, oil company executives could be held accountable in such cases. Image via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law. The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation, ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”
For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations. Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “digital nation” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago. In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment. As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu, says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations.
Tuvulu’s Foreign Minister delivers an address to COP26, while standing in knee-deep water to illustrate how rising sea levels threaten Pacific nations. Image from Simon Kofe’s Facebook. Fair use.

It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis. These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S., China, and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.

Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible. This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.
Vanuatu was the first state to call for ecocide to be added to the ICC in 2019. In announcing the proposal, Regenvanu said:

“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC. Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”
A protest poster against ecocide shaming oil giants at a climate protest in Maryland in 2017. Photo from Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

Environmental crimes are particularly tricky, as traditional legal accountability measures tend to rely on specific individuals or property that have been harmed in order to pursue legal action. In cases where polluters are contributing to a broader destructive pattern, the legal standing becomes murky. This theory has been tested numerous times as individuals have sought to sue fossil fuel companies in civil court for their destructive practices and malfeasance, with most cases largely unsuccessful.

Supporters say that if the proposed amendment were successful, it would give ICC prosecutors the power to hold individuals, such as the executives of large polluting companies or heads of state, responsible in cases like massive oil spills or the deforestation of essential rainforests.
As an editorial in The Global Witness notes:

While there have been a series of recent valiant attempts to sue fossil fuel corporations in civil court for covering up evidence that their activities were causing global warming, the defendants have largely been able to get away scot-free. … Criminalizing ecocide would fill this legal gap, and allow individuals (and companies in some jurisdictions) to be prosecuted for engaging in acts with knowledge that they are substantially likely to damage the environment, without the need to show harm to any individual person.

To add a crime to the Rome Statute, a proposal must win a two-thirds majority vote within the court’s Assembly of States Parties. Even then, an amendment to the statute’s crimes provisions would bind only the states that accept it, and the court could not prosecute nationals or territory of states that do not.

The Rome Statute has 123 signatory parties — a number that does not include China, India, or the U.S., the world’s three largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S., in particular, under current President Donald Trump’s administration, has backed away from climate commitments in recent years, including withdrawing from the UN’s 2015 Paris Climate Agreement. It has also become increasingly hostile toward the court itself, as the Trump administration imposed sanctions on individual ICC prosecutors and judges beginning in early 2025. Then, in a September 2026 address to the UN General Assembly, Trump urged all member states to withdraw from the treaty altogether, and, weeks later, in October 2026, he imposed sweeping sanctions on the court itself.

With the biggest emitters outside the court, and Washington working to undermine it, advocates are looking beyond The Hague and ICC reform. As legal watchdogs argue, the end goal is not merely to get the ICC to recognize ecocide — though that would be an excellent first step — rather, if the ICC were to establish a framework for prosecuting international environmental crimes, through an amendment or merely by adapting its existing policies, this could push ratifying states to update their domestic penal codes and adopt policies to protect and preserve their own ecosystems, and also prosecute those who violate them.
Existing provisions within the Rome Statute
The International Criminal Court (ICC) at The Hague. Photo via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 2.0.
Even though the proposal has thus far not been adopted by the ICC, the court has not stood still.

In December 2025, ICC prosecutors published a policy paper on prosecuting environmental damage through the pre-existing mechanisms already laid out in the Rome Statute — the international treaty which established the ICC.

The Rome Statute mentions the environment exactly one time. Article 8(2)(b)(iv) makes it a war crime to launch an attack knowing it will cause “widespread, long-term and severe” damage to the environment. Traditionally, this article has applied only during armed conflict, and previous attempts to prosecute environmental destruction at the court have been unsuccessful.
Vanuatu’s ambassador to the UN, Odo Tevi, has argued that the reckless destruction of nature “can and does take place at any time, not just during conflict.”

The December 2025 policy, launched at the Assembly of States Parties, was co-hosted by Costa Rica, France, Germany, Panama, and the Marshall Islands. It explains how environmental destruction can be investigated and prosecuted within the four existing crime categories, for example, when pollution or the seizure of natural resources is used to commit a crime against humanity.

Analysts at the Conflict and Environment Observatory note that this policy paper does not address the ecocide proposal and that ambiguity in the war crime standard remains. Others point to limited resources at the prosecutor’s office.

In September 2026, ICC representatives said they had “moved into the implementation stage” to establish clearer parameters for prosecuting environmental crimes under the Rome Statute. In its statement, the office said it had received numerous communications about alleged crimes with an environmental dimension and was building a network of environmental law enforcement authorities, relevant organizations, expert groups, and civil society organizations to investigate.

But some jurisdictions are not waiting. As one recent study notes, “the substance of ecocide criminalization has advanced everywhere except through the amendment: an EU directive whose gravest offense is officially ‘comparable to “ecocide,”’ a Council of Europe convention, national codes in Belgium, France and Ukraine, and a completed OTP [ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor] policy that prosecutes environmental damage through the existing four crimes.”

Counts vary depending on how many states currently employ domestic laws against ecocide. Stop Ecocide International says twelve countries, including Belgium, France, and Ukraine, have adopted ecocide or equivalent offenses into domestic law. Mauritius became the most recent in April 2026, and legislation is progressing in countries including Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Mexico, Italy, and the Netherlands.

As noted in the aforementioned study, the EU’s revised Environmental Crime Directive also covers conduct “comparable to ecocide,” and member states had to transpose it by May 2026. Additionally, legal and environmental experts from 14 Latin American countries published a model ecocide law on October 1, 2026, in an effort to jumpstart future ecocide laws in the region.

The next stage is procedural rather than dramatic: Whether states give the proposal a formal path forward at the Assembly of States Parties’ 25th session in The Hague, from November 30 to December 7, 2026. A vote would signal whether the Rome Statute can grow beyond the atrocities it was written for. A stall would leave the prosecutor’s policy and national laws as the main tools available.
The decision comes at a crucial time for the ICC, as some international stakeholders begin to question the legitimacy, power, and effectiveness of international ruling bodies.

For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them. Until that infrastructure is implemented, the burden of harm will continue to fall on those least responsible for causing this crisis.

articles.title: Why Japan’s anti-hate measures fall short
articles.author: Jo Carter
paras: Japan is yet to establish the Human Rights Protection Bill and a independent national human rights institution
Originally published on Global Voices
Anti-immigration policy protest in Oct 2026. Screen capture from the Japan Unfiltered YouTube Channel. Fair Use

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
A newborn Black baby delivered at a clinic in Tokyo’s Meguro Ward became the target of a barrage of racist harassment online.

The clinic published the baby’s photo with a congratulatory message on its social media account as part of its routine “babies born this month” photo series. A screenshot of the post spread widely on X, gaining more than 1.3 million views within a day. The post attracted many hateful comments loaded with anti-immigrant sentiment and racial discrimination against non-white and non-Japanese people. Some of the hateful comments received thousands of likes.
All comments have since been removed from the post, and the clinic has disabled commenting on its Instagram.

This incident sheds light on two issues within Japanese society. On one level, it reflects how racist hate speech still remains rampant in Japan. But more broadly, it exposes a missing layer of justice infrastructure: Japan has no independent human rights commission empowered to handle discrimination complaints, no enforceable national hate speech law, and no effective way to force platforms to remove hate speech targeting entire groups.

While some cultural critics argue that the widespread racial discrimination in Japan stems from the younger generation’s inadequate interest in foreign cultures and development, others argue that the prevalence of online hate speech is to a large extent related to a lack of effective domestic legislation and human rights education.

Despite being a signatory to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) since 1995, Japan has not passed the Human Rights Protection Bill or established an independent national human rights institution to investigate human rights violations and penalize perpetrators. While there have been numerous attempts to pass such a bill, it was tabled multiple times in the 2000s and early 2010s. Critics say the efforts failed because the public feared it could violate the freedom of speech protected by the Constitution.
Toothless anti-discrimination national laws

Thus, instead of passing a comprehensive set of laws, it addresses discrimination and human rights through issue-specific laws, such as the Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Human Rights Awareness-Raising (2000), the Act for Eliminating Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (2013), the Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behavior against Persons with Countries of Origin other than Japan (2016), the Act on the Promotion of the Elimination of Buraku Discrimination (2016), as well as the Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (2023), which aim to raise public awareness about human rights and providing government support rather than criminalizing hate speech and discrimination.

For example, while the Hate Speech Elimination Act was enacted to curb xenophobic street rallies that terrify ethnic minorities residing in Japan, such as the series of protests against Kyoto Korean Elementary School between December 2009 and March 2010, it does not declare hate speech illegal, nor penalize offenders with fines or jail sentences.

Moreover, the law only protects foreigners with a legal status, but excludes undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and Indigenous peoples, including the Ainu and Ryūkyūans. The law’s legal scope is at odds with the United Nations’ recommendations, which state that a signatory of the ICERD must “ensure legislative guarantees against racial discrimination apply to non-citizens regardless of their immigration status, and that the implementation of legislation does not have a discriminatory effect on non-citizens.” Legal experts have criticized the restrictive clause of the law for, as Shuji Oda, president of the Dai-Ichi Tokyo Bar Association, says, “giving rise to a false reverse implication that hate speech directed at individuals without legal residency status is permissible.”

The toothless anti-discrimination laws only manage to contain explicit discriminatory actions against disabled people, Burakumin (feudal outcasts), LGBTQ+ people, and foreigners with legal status; they have not eliminated hate speech. Meanwhile, street rallies against immigrant and imported labor have surged amid stagnant local wages, inflation, and rising living costs. Though these protests are usually small in scale, they attract a large number of social media comments, with plenty of discriminatory remarks and hate speech against foreigners.

Additionally, none of the aforementioned laws has a mechanism to force internet platforms to remove harmful content; this results in the spread of xenophobia, homophobia, hatred against social minorities, and a racist online culture.

As Japanese national politics has stalled the enactment of the Human Rights Protection Bill, some local governments have started building the legal framework from the bottom up to address local unrest targeting ethnic minorities.

Kawasaki City, which is home to a large Zainichi Korean population in Kanagawa Prefecture, was the first municipality in Japan to introduce punitive local laws to curb protests that “injure the human dignity of others,” as described by the city’s Justice Department.

Since the national Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Awareness was passed in 2000, the city enacted its own Children’s Rights Ordinance in 2000 and Human Rights Ombudsperson Ordinance in 2001, which paved the way for the establishment of a local independent Human Rights Ombudsperson system for receiving and investigating complaints on bullying, abuse, and discrimination.

Following a surge of demonstrations calling for the exclusion of people of foreign origin around 2013, the city enacted the Ordinance for the Creation of a City that Respects Human Rights and is Free from Discrimination in December 2019, which prohibits discrimination based on race, nationality, ethnic origin, gender, sexual orientation, and disability. The ordinance also bans using loudspeakers, placards, or flyers that induce hatred against people originating from outside Japan and their descendants. Under the Ordinance, repeat offenders would have their identities publicly disclosed, and they could be fined up to JPY 500,000 (approximately USD 3,130). The city would also keep a record of hate groups and ban them from using public facilities, such as sports venues and parks.

Furthermore, the ordinance established an expert panel empowered to review hate speech and instruct online platforms to remove extreme content targeting a specific group of people and disclose the abusers’ identities.

While the ordinance has managed to reduce discriminatory protests against Korean-Japanese communities within Kawasaki City, it is powerless when the protests take place in neighboring jurisdictions. Moreover, thus far the criminal penalty of the local ordinance just punishes abusers targeting people originating from outside of Japan; LGBTQ+, disabled, and indigenous communities have remained unprotected. It cannot penalize landlords or employers who discriminate and has limited power over online abuse, as internet companies are not legally bound by local laws.
Human rights education translated into moral education

Various UN bodies have repeatedly criticized Japan for failing to enact a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and establish an independent commission to investigate and prosecute abusers in line with the “Paris Principle,” the official international standards for national human rights institutions. Yet, to date, Japanese society still lacks the consensus and determination to pass the Human Rights Protection Bill.
While proponents of stalling the legislation cite potential violations of free speech, a deeper reason relates to local xenophobia and perceptions of human rights.

The concept of human rights was introduced to Japan about 150 years ago, during the Japanese modernization period beginning in the late Edo and early Meiji era. However, when the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was promulgated in 1889, it defined citizens’ rights not as inherent human rights, but as “rights of subjects” granted by the Emperor.

Only after World War II was the concept of universal human rights re-introduced and localized to criticize Japan’s wartime militarization of society and crimes against non-Japanese people. Yet, human rights education in schools is often confused with conventional moral education, which emphasizes individual responsibility to family, society, and the country, and the need to maintain harmonious human relations through interpersonal politeness and consideration.

However, the individual morality approach overlooks the structural causes of discrimination and fails to empower individuals as rights-holders to address the problem of systematic discrimination, as pointed out by a group of Japanese teachers from the Institute of Global Education and Culture in a proposal to better integrate moral and human rights education in 2014:
日本では人権教育・啓発の場で「おもいやり」「やさしさ」などが強調される一方で、権利そのものを学習することは低調である。[…] […]具体的な「権利」という側面も、また「社会的に」問題を解決しようという側面も極めて弱い。「思いやり」を強調する抽象的・心情主義的教育は、私的な人間関係の中での問題解決ばかりを強調し、権利を具体的に考え実現しようとする力をむしろ弱めているといえる。

In Japan, human rights education and awareness-raising campaigns have kept emphasising concepts like ‘consideration for others’ (omoi-yari) and ‘kindness’ while downplaying education on rights. […] It’s extremely weak in addressing different aspects of individual rights and the social resolution of rights-related problems. The emphasis on ‘understanding’ is both abstract and sentimental; as such, education relies solely on problem-solving within private interpersonal relationships and will hence weaken the ability to think concretely about rights and exercising one’s rights.

Earlier this year, Human Rights Watch urged the newly elected prime minister Sanae Takaichi to legislate a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and create an independent national human rights body to address the rise of xenophobic sentiments against immigrants. Although the right-leaning government has no intention of resurrecting the Human Rights Protection Bill, a civic coalition has formed to advocate for an independent National Human Rights Institution with investigative and corrective powers to address discrimination and human rights abuses by 2028.

articles.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
articles.author: Martin Steven, Senior Lecturer, School of Global Affairs, Lancaster University
paras: Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.
Burnham is walking a fine line

Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.
At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

Martin Steven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Family stories keep alive Georgia’s democratic past and the memory of Soviet repression
articles.author: Daria Dergacheva
paras: In the Guria region, an organization is helping people recover a history the Soviets tried to erase
Originally published on Global Voices
Resort in the Guria region of Georgia. Photo by Tinari.totoro on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country. It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south. It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.
Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low. However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.
This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.
Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM): Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia. We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life. We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies. We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present. We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

LM: One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold. These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union. Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after World War II. As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904. Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities. The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important. We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

LM: Through the project ‘From Understanding the Past to the Digital Future,’ implemented from April to October 2026, we organized several activities across the three municipalities of Guria: Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. Our main activities included a public discussion. On June 24, we organized ‘What Drove Gurians Crazy? Propaganda Now and Then,’ exploring Guria’s democratic history, Soviet occupation, propaganda, and contemporary challenges. We also did digital storytelling workshops, an AI and Digital Creation workshop and a theatrical performance: on August 12, we presented “My Days and My Father’s Diaries,” dedicated to Meri Chanukvadze and her father, Amberki Chanukvadze, whose life reflected the impact of Soviet repression. These activities helped strengthen participants’ digital skills, encourage historical research, and create opportunities for community members to share their stories online.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

LM: The project generated strong interest across all three municipalities, reaching nearly 50 community members, with particularly strong participation from women and young people. Locals participated in the digital storytelling workshop, including 12 women. These activities gave participants practical opportunities to develop their digital skills and explore new ways of communicating important ideas. Another meaningful example was the theatrical performance dedicated to Meri and her father. More than 35 people attended and participated in a discussion afterwards. The performance encouraged people to reflect on the experiences of families affected by Soviet repression and the importance of preserving historical memory. The project also laid the foundation for a cross-municipal network of young people, activists, and aspiring digital storytellers. This network can help community members continue documenting local history, sharing civic information, and engaging in public discussions beyond the project itself.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

LM: Our participation in the project strengthened our understanding of how digital technologies can support civic engagement and democratic participation. We gained greater awareness of the importance of digital storytelling, media literacy, and critical thinking in helping communities understand their history and respond to contemporary challenges. We also explored how AI-assisted content creation can provide new opportunities for preserving local stories and making them accessible to wider audiences. The project reinforced our belief that digital tools are not simply communication technologies; they can also help people participate in public life, challenge misinformation, and contribute to community development. Most importantly, we recognized that connecting historical memory with modern digital tools can help create a more informed, active, and engaged society.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

LM: One of the most valuable lessons was that many people are interested in learning about their history when they are given a welcoming space to ask questions and share experiences. Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility. We also learned that practical workshops and collaborative activities are effective ways to introduce digital tools to community members. The strong participation of women and young people demonstrated the potential for inclusive, community-based learning. Another important lesson was the value of combining traditional storytelling with digital technologies. Personal stories, family diaries, public discussions, and theatrical performances can make historical events more relatable and meaningful.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

LM: We plan to build on the experience and connections developed through the project by continuing to document, digitize, and share historical and civic stories from Guria. We aim to encourage more community members, especially young people and women, to use digital storytelling and online content creation to preserve family histories and discuss local issues. We also intend to apply the knowledge gained from the workshops to future educational activities, community discussions, and collaborative initiatives. An important priority will be to strengthen the network of local journalists, activists, and digital storytellers across Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. By supporting collaboration and knowledge-sharing, we hope to ensure that these activities continue beyond the project period.

articles.title: Support Global Voices’ December Spotlight: Digital Communities
articles.author: Global Voices Announcements
paras: Donate to our Digital Communities Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Images via Canva and public domain.

Digital communications sparked new ways of forming communities: communities that spanned vast distances; that offered asynchronous interaction, innovative forms of constructing identities, and potentially enormous reach. These communities have provided connection for people who are isolated or marginalized, built powerful groups around both professional interests and unusual hobbies, and facilitated astonishing feats of knowledge-sharing and organizing, from Wikipedia to academic sub-field networks to hobby groups and fandoms.

But digital communities bring new challenges as well, from questions of moderation to questions of ownership. Almost all of them are built on the backbone of infrastructure owned by Big Tech — hardware at a minimum, usually several layers of software as well.

This is a risky place to put trust. Witness the sudden devastation when a platform is bought and sold, and what was accessible and inclusive becomes hostile; or the sudden change-to-terms-of-service maneuver, when a company leverages the trust of its users to exploit them for their sellable data. Increasingly hollowed-out echo chambers — toxic or just obliviously navel-gazing — make digital communities difficult and often dangerous to navigate. The proliferation of targeted ads, the risks of rapidly spreading mis- and disinformation, and, more recently, the insertion of large language model bots all illustrate this.

Sometimes it feels like it’s impossible to resist the tidal wave of AI slop and bot content and the all-pervasive mistrust of information engendered by the sheer amount of misinformation and disinformation we have seen produced this decade. But there are still ways to organize digitally.

The same social media that is polarizing Indian society is where young people have organized and continued to organize to resist the authoritarian Modi government. In Brazil, supporters of President Lula ran an organic, human-driven campaign that successfully beat algorithms weighted toward his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the October 2026 election. LGBTQ+ people in hostile environments often only have online spaces to find community and solidarity. People everywhere are rewilding the internet, reclaiming, reviving, and rebuilding communities everywhere in defiance of faceless, consolidated power.

In this month’s spotlight, Global Voices, in partnership with Ranking Digital Rights, will explore the multiverse of digital communities — starting with our own. We want to highlight specific communities, the tools and tactics they use to organize, resist, and overcome the algorithmic pressure from tech platforms, and show how digital communities thrive and persist the world over, defying overwhelming power asymmetries and rejecting pressure to accept the defaults.
